rendering.convention: All mathematical expressions (ordered pairs, set-builder notation, function notation, modulus/GIF/signum notation, domain-range interval notation, etc.) are rendered as KaTeX-compatible LaTeX wrapped in \( ... \) inline delimiters. Plain HTML sub/sup is used only for genuinely trivial numeric subscripts outside of any math expression. No raw Unicode math symbols are used anywhere in question, option, explanation, hint, or concept-card text. Rendering requires a KaTeX auto-render pass (or equivalent) on the client, configured to scan for \( \) inline delimiters.

topics.name: Cartesian Product of Sets
topics.summary: An ordered pair \((a,b)\) has a fixed order, so \((a,b)=(c,d)\) only when \(a=c\) and \(b=d\) — \((2,3)\) and \((3,2)\) are different pairs. The Cartesian product \(A \times B\) is the set of every ordered pair with the first entry from \(A\) and the second from \(B\): \(A \times B = \{(a,b): a \in A, b \in B\}\). Its size is always \(n(A \times B) = n(A) \times n(B)\), never a sum, and it is empty whenever either set is empty. In general \(A \times B \ne B \times A\) unless \(A=B\), since swapping the sets swaps every pair's components. This idea is the foundation for everything that follows in the chapter: a relation is defined as a subset of \(A \times B\), and a function is a special kind of relation, so a firm grip on ordered pairs and their counting formula pays off throughout.
topics.worked_example: If \(A=\{1,2\}\) and \(B=\{3,4\}\), then \(A \times B = \{(1,3),(1,4),(2,3),(2,4)\}\), and indeed \(n(A \times B) = 2 \times 2 = 4\) matches the count of pairs listed.
common_mistakes: Adding \(n(A)\) and \(n(B)\) instead of multiplying them.
Confusing \(A \times B\) with \(B \times A\) — the pairs are reversed, not the same set.
Treating an ordered pair like an unordered set, i.e. assuming \((a,b)=(b,a)\).
Forgetting to apply an extra algebraic condition (like an inequality) before counting or listing the pairs.

topics.name: Relations — Definition, Domain, Co-domain & Range
topics.summary: A relation \(R\) from \(A\) to \(B\) is simply any subset of \(A \times B\) — a chosen collection of ordered pairs, possibly following a stated rule such as \(R=\{(x,y): y=x^2\}\). Three sets matter here and are easy to mix up: the domain is only the first-coordinates that actually appear in \(R\); the co-domain is the entire target set \(B\) that was declared at the outset, whether or not every element of it is used; and the range is only the second-coordinates that actually appear in \(R\), which is always a subset of the co-domain (and can be a proper subset). The total number of relations that can be formed from \(A\) to \(B\) is \(2^{n(A) \times n(B)}\), since each of the \(n(A)\times n(B)\) possible pairs can independently be included or excluded; subtract \(1\) if the empty relation should not be counted.
key_formulas: \(\text{Number of relations from } A \text{ to } B = 2^{\,n(A)\times n(B)}\)
topics.worked_example: For \(A=\{1,2,3\}\) and \(R=\{(x,y): x,y \in A,\, y=x+1\}\): checking each \(x\) gives \(R=\{(1,2),(2,3)\}\), so the domain is \(\{1,2\}\) and the range is \(\{2,3\}\) — note \(3\) never appears as a first coordinate, so it is in the range but not the domain.
common_mistakes: Confusing the range (values actually attained) with the co-domain (the whole declared target set).
Reporting the domain when the range was asked for, or vice versa.
Forgetting to check an additional restriction in a set-builder rule (like \(y \le 5\)) before listing every pair.
Using the wrong exponent when counting relations — it is \(n(A)\times n(B)\), not \(n(A)+n(B)\) or \(n(A)\) alone.

topics.name: Representing Relations (Roster, Set-Builder, Arrow Diagram)
topics.summary: The same relation can be written three ways. Roster form lists every ordered pair explicitly, e.g. \(\{(1,2),(2,4),(3,6)\}\). Set-builder form states the defining rule instead, e.g. \(\{(x,y): y=2x,\, x \in \{1,2,3\}\}\) — the same relation, written compactly. Arrow diagrams show two ovals for \(A\) and \(B\) with arrows drawn from each related \(a \in A\) to its \(b \in B\). Converting between these forms is mostly bookkeeping: from a rule, evaluate it at every allowed input and keep only outputs that land inside the stated set; from an arrow diagram, the domain is every element with an outgoing arrow and the range is every element with an incoming arrow — not necessarily the whole of \(B\). A common trap when converting is applying an extra condition (an inequality, a divisibility rule) only partway through the list.
key_formulas: \(R = \{(a,b): a \in A,\, b \in B,\, \text{condition on } a,b\}\)
topics.worked_example: \(R=\{(x,y): y=2x-1,\, x \in \{2,3,4,5\}\}\) converts to roster form as \(\{(2,3),(3,5),(4,7),(5,9)\}\) by substituting each allowed \(x\) into the rule.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to check that a rule's output actually lands inside the stated co-domain before including a pair.
Swapping the \(x\) and \(y\) components when moving between representations.
Reading the range off an arrow diagram as the whole of \(B\), instead of only the elements that are actually hit by an arrow.
Stopping the roster list early and missing later pairs that still satisfy the rule.

topics.name: Functions — Definition, Domain, Co-domain & Range
topics.summary: A function \(f: A \to B\) is a relation with one extra requirement: every element of the domain \(A\) must have exactly one image in \(B\) — no element is left unmapped, and none is mapped to two different outputs. When a function is given by a formula rather than a set, finding its domain means finding every real \(x\) for which the formula actually produces a real number: exclude values that make a denominator zero, and require the expression under an even root to be non-negative (strictly positive if that root itself sits in a denominator). When a formula has several such restrictions, the domain is their intersection, not their union. The range is the actual set of outputs, which for algebraic expressions is often found by simplifying, completing the square, or checking behaviour at endpoints and turning points.
topics.worked_example: For \(f(x)=\sqrt{x-2}\), the domain needs \(x-2\ge0\), i.e. \(x\ge2\), so the domain is \([2,\infty)\); since the square root is never negative, the range is \([0,\infty)\).
common_mistakes: Combining two domain restrictions with union instead of intersection.
Using \(\ge\) where \(>\) is required (or vice versa) at a boundary point.
Assuming any relation given by a formula is automatically a function without checking the one-output-per-input requirement.
Treating the co-domain stated in the problem as if it were the actual range.

topics.name: Real-Valued Functions — Identity, Constant & Polynomial Functions
topics.summary: Three named families of real functions recur throughout the chapter. The identity function \(f(x)=x\) maps every real number to itself. A constant function \(f(x)=c\) maps every input to the same fixed output, so its range is a single value — even when the constant is disguised inside an expression that algebraically simplifies down to a number. A polynomial function is any \(f(x)=a_nx^n+\cdots+a_1x+a_0\); evaluating one at a point is direct substitution, but finding its range over a restricted domain needs more care — for a quadratic, the range depends on whether the vertex (\(x=-b/2a\)) lies inside the given interval, since that is where the extreme value actually occurs, not necessarily at the endpoints. A quadratic with a positive leading coefficient opens upward, so its vertex (when inside the interval) gives the minimum of the range, while the larger of the two endpoint values gives the maximum; a negative leading coefficient flips this, making the vertex a maximum instead. Recognising which case applies before evaluating anything saves a lot of avoidable sign confusion.
topics.worked_example: For \(f(x)=x^2-4x+3\) on \([0,5]\), the vertex \(x=2\) lies inside the interval and gives the minimum \(f(2)=-1\); comparing the endpoints \(f(0)=3\) and \(f(5)=8\) gives the maximum \(8\), so the range is \([-1,8]\).
common_mistakes: Checking only the endpoints of an interval and forgetting the vertex can give a more extreme value.
Missing that a negative leading coefficient turns the vertex into a maximum, not a minimum.
Failing to notice when an expression algebraically simplifies to a constant.
Sign slips when substituting a value into a polynomial with several terms.

topics.name: Rational, Modulus, Signum & Greatest Integer Functions
topics.summary: Several standard functions are built from cases rather than a single formula. A rational function \(f(x)=p(x)/q(x)\) is undefined wherever \(q(x)=0\). The modulus function is \(|x|=x\) for \(x\ge0\) and \(|x|=-x\) for \(x<0\) — always non-negative. The signum function returns only the sign of the input: \(1\) if \(x>0\), \(0\) if \(x=0\), and \(-1\) if \(x<0\). The greatest integer function \([x]\) (also called the floor function) returns the largest integer not exceeding \(x\); it stays constant across each interval \([n,n+1)\) and jumps by \(1\) at every integer, which is why \([x]\) rounds *down* even for negative numbers — \([-2.5]=-3\), not \(-2\). Because it stays flat across a whole unit interval, an equation like \([x]=n\) is satisfied by every \(x\) in \([n,n+1)\), not by a single value, and this same interval-thinking is what makes domain restrictions involving \([x]\) remove a whole stretch of the number line rather than just one isolated point.
topics.worked_example: To evaluate \([x]+|x|\) at \(x=-2.5\): \([-2.5]=-3\) (floor, not round-toward-zero) and \(|-2.5|=2.5\), so the sum is \(-3+2.5=-0.5\).
common_mistakes: Rounding \([x]\) toward zero for negative non-integers instead of flooring it downward.
Dropping the outer modulus sign, leaving an answer negative when it should be positive.
Treating \([x]=n\) as describing the single point \(x=n\) rather than the whole interval \([n,n+1)\).
Forgetting that \(|x|-a=0\)-type conditions exclude two points (\(x=\pm a\)), not just one.

topics.name: Algebra of Real Functions (Sum, Difference, Product, Quotient, Scalar Multiple)
topics.summary: Given two real functions \(f\) and \(g\), new functions can be built pointwise: \((f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)\), \((f-g)(x)=f(x)-g(x)\), \((fg)(x)=f(x)g(x)\), \((f/g)(x)=f(x)/g(x)\), and for a scalar \(k\), \((kf)(x)=k\cdot f(x)\). The domain of a sum, difference, or product is the intersection of the two individual domains — never their union, since a point must be valid for both functions to combine them there. For a quotient, one more restriction applies on top of that intersection: every point where \(g(x)=0\) must also be excluded, since division by zero is undefined. To evaluate a combined function at a specific point, it is usually easiest to evaluate \(f\) and \(g\) separately first, then combine the two numbers — trying to simplify the combined expression symbolically before substituting tends to invite avoidable slips. The same care applies to a scalar multiple \(kf\): its domain is unchanged from that of \(f\) alone, since multiplying by a constant never introduces a new restriction.
common_mistakes: Taking the union of the two domains instead of their intersection.
Forgetting to additionally exclude the zeros of \(g\) when forming \(f/g\).
Reversing the order in a subtraction, computing \(g(x)-f(x)\) instead of \(f(x)-g(x)\).
Multiplying when the operation was addition, or vice versa, when evaluating at a specific point.

topics.name: Graphs of Real Functions & Their Interpretation
topics.summary: Reading a function's graph gives its domain (the spread of \(x\)-values covered) and range (the spread of \(y\)-values covered) directly, and shows visually why a vertical line crossing the graph more than once means it is not the graph of a function. Where two graphs \(y=f(x)\) and \(y=g(x)\) intersect corresponds exactly to the solutions of the equation \(f(x)=g(x)\), so intersection-counting problems reduce to solving that equation and counting the valid real solutions. Care is needed with piecewise graphs like \(y=|x|\) or \(y=[x]\): solving the case-split equation algebraically can produce extra roots that don't actually satisfy the sign condition of their own case, and these spurious roots must be rejected before counting the true number of intersection points. It also helps to notice symmetry early: if both graphs being compared are even functions, any positive-side solution guarantees a mirror solution on the negative side, and forgetting to count that mirror point is one of the most common ways to undercount an intersection problem.
key_formulas: \(\text{intersections of } y=f(x) \text{ and } y=g(x): \text{ solve } f(x)=g(x)\)
topics.worked_example: For \(y=|x|\) and \(y=x+2\): the case \(x\ge0\) gives no solution, while the case \(x<0\) gives \(x=-1\) (valid, since \(-1<0\)), so the graphs intersect in exactly \(1\) point.
common_mistakes: Accepting an algebraic root without checking it satisfies the sign condition of the case it came from.
Missing the symmetric negative-side root when both functions involved are even.
Confusing the number of algebraic roots of an equation with the number of genuine intersection points.
Reading the co-domain of a piecewise graph as its range, instead of only the values actually traced out.

questions.question: For two non-empty sets \(A\) and \(B\), the Cartesian product \(A \times B\) is defined as the set of all:
options: elements that belong to \(A\) or \(B\) or both
unordered pairs \(\{a,b\}\) with \(a \in A,\, b \in B\)
ordered pairs \((a,b)\) with \(a \in A,\, b \in B\)
questions.explanation: \(A \times B = \{(a,b) : a \in A,\, b \in B\}\) — it is the set of all ordered pairs formed by taking the first component from \(A\) and the second from \(B\).
questions.hint: The word 'ordered' is the key — position matters here, unlike in a set.
distractor_logic: confuses Cartesian product with set union
confuses Cartesian product with set intersection
confuses the ordered pair \((a,b)\) with the unordered set \(\{a,b\}\)

questions.question: Two ordered pairs \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\) are equal if and only if:
options: at least one of \(a=c\) or \(b=d\) holds
questions.explanation: Ordered pairs are equal exactly when their corresponding components match: \((a,b)=(c,d) \iff a=c \text{ and } b=d\).
questions.hint: Compare position by position — first with first, second with second.
distractor_logic: requires only one match instead of both, which is too weak a condition
swaps which component must match which — this would make \((2,3)\) equal to \((3,2)\)
uses a sum condition, which many unequal pairs could still satisfy

questions.question: If \(n(A) = p\) and \(n(B) = q\), then \(n(A \times B)\) equals:
questions.explanation: Each of the \(p\) elements of \(A\) can be paired with each of the \(q\) elements of \(B\), giving \(n(A \times B) = n(A) \times n(B) = pq\).
questions.hint: Think of it as filling two independent slots — first slot has \(p\) choices, second has \(q\) choices.
distractor_logic: introduces a stray factor of 2 with no basis
mistakes it for an exponent rule that doesn't apply here
confuses the counting rule for \(A \times B\) with that for \(A \cup B\) (which uses addition, and even that needs an overlap correction)

questions.question: If \(A = \emptyset\) or \(B = \emptyset\), then \(A \times B\) is:
questions.explanation: By convention, the Cartesian product with an empty set is always empty: \(A \times \emptyset = \emptyset \times B = \emptyset\), since there are no elements available to form a pair from the empty side.
questions.hint: You need an element from both sets to build even one ordered pair.
distractor_logic: mistakenly returns the non-empty set \(B\) itself instead of the empty set
mistakenly returns the non-empty set \(A\) itself instead of the empty set
treats the product as undefined rather than recognising it is simply empty

questions.question: For non-empty, unequal sets \(A\) and \(B\), which statement about \(A \times B\) and \(B \times A\) is correct?
options: In general \(A \times B \neq B \times A\), though both have the same number of elements
questions.explanation: The Cartesian product is not commutative — \((a,b) \in A \times B\) has \(a\) from \(A\) first, while in \(B \times A\) an element of \(B\) comes first, so the pairs generally differ, even though \(n(A\times B) = n(B \times A) = n(A)n(B)\).
questions.hint: Check order: is \((a,b)\) the same ordered pair as \((b,a)\)?
distractor_logic: wrongly assumes Cartesian product behaves like ordinary multiplication of numbers, which is commutative
confuses equal cardinality (which does always hold) with equality of the sets themselves
overcorrects and assumes no overlap between the two products is ever possible, which isn't the question being asked

questions.question: A relation \(R\) from a non-empty set \(A\) to a non-empty set \(B\) is defined as:
options: any subset of \(A\) whose elements also lie in \(B\)
questions.explanation: A relation from \(A\) to \(B\) is simply any subset of the Cartesian product \(A \times B\) — it need not pair every element, and an element can be paired with more than one image.
questions.hint: Every relation lives inside the set of all possible ordered pairs, \(A \times B\).
distractor_logic: describes something closer to \(A \cap B\) and ignores that a relation is built from ordered pairs, not raw elements
confuses relations with the stricter notion of a function, for which every element must additionally have exactly one image
confuses \(A \times B\) (ordered pairs) with \(A \cup B\) (a union of raw elements, not pairs)

questions.question: For a relation \(R\) from \(A\) to \(B\), the domain of \(R\) is:
options: the set of all second components of the ordered pairs in \(R\)
the set of all first components of the ordered pairs in \(R\)
questions.explanation: The domain of a relation is the set of all first elements of the ordered pairs that belong to it: \(\text{Domain}(R) = \{a : (a,b) \in R\}\).
questions.hint: Domain looks at the 'input' side — the first coordinate of each pair.
distractor_logic: confuses the domain of a relation with the entire product set it is drawn from
swaps domain (first components) with range (second components)
confuses domain with the co-domain \(B\)

questions.question: If a relation \(R\) is from set \(A\) to set \(B\), then the co-domain of \(R\) is:
options: the set \(B\), regardless of which elements are actually used as images
the set of second components that actually appear in \(R\)
always equal to the range of \(R\)
questions.explanation: The co-domain is the entire target set \(B\) that \(R\) is defined into, whether or not every element of \(B\) is actually used as an image. The range, by contrast, is only the second components that actually appear — so \(\text{Range}(R) \subseteq \text{Co-domain}(R)\), not necessarily equal.
questions.hint: Co-domain is fixed by how \(R\) is declared ('from \(A\) to \(B\)'); range depends on which pairs are actually in \(R\).
distractor_logic: confuses co-domain with domain, mixing up which set is the source and which is the target
describes the range, not the co-domain
wrongly claims co-domain and range are always identical, when range can be a proper subset

questions.question: If \(n(A) = m\) and \(n(B) = n\), the total number of relations that can be defined from \(A\) to \(B\) (including the empty relation) is:
questions.explanation: A relation from \(A\) to \(B\) is any subset of \(A \times B\), which has \(mn\) elements. A set with \(k\) elements has \(2^k\) subsets, so the number of relations is \(2^{mn}\).
questions.hint: First find \(n(A \times B)\), then use the 'a set with \(k\) elements has \(2^k\) subsets' rule.
distractor_logic: gives only \(n(A \times B)\) itself, forgetting to count all its subsets
uses the right subset-counting idea but on the wrong base number (\(m+n\) instead of \(mn\))
adds instead of multiplying to get the size of \(A \times B\) in the first place

questions.question: The empty set \(\emptyset\), regarded as a relation from \(A\) to \(B\), is called the:
questions.explanation: Since \(\emptyset \subseteq A \times B\) for any sets \(A\), \(B\), the empty set is itself a valid relation, called the void or empty relation — it relates no element of \(A\) to any element of \(B\).
questions.hint: This is the relation that contains no ordered pairs at all.
distractor_logic: names a specific relation on a single set (pairing each element with itself), which is unrelated to the empty relation
names the relation obtained by swapping components of every pair, which doesn't describe the empty case
names the opposite extreme — the relation that is all of \(A \times B\), not none of it

questions.question: A relation between finite sets can be represented in which of the following ways?
options: Roster form, set-builder form, and an arrow diagram
questions.explanation: A relation between finite sets can be shown by listing its ordered pairs (roster form), by stating the defining rule (set-builder form), or by drawing arrows from elements of \(A\) to their images in \(B\) (arrow diagram) — all three describe the same relation.
questions.hint: NCERT presents three standard representations for a relation between finite sets.
distractor_logic: names only one of the three standard forms
omits the arrow diagram, which is a standard representation for relations between finite sets
names only one of the three standard forms

questions.question: Writing a relation as \(R = \{(1,2), (2,4), (3,6)\}\) is an example of representing it in:
questions.explanation: Listing out every ordered pair that belongs to the relation, as done here, is called the roster (or list) form of the relation.
questions.hint: Roster form means simply listing the elements/pairs, the way you'd list elements of a set.
distractor_logic: confuses roster form with set-builder form, which instead states a defining rule such as \(y=2x\)
invents a term that isn't one of the three standard representations
confuses a written listing with a diagram, which is a visual representation, not a listing

questions.question: The set-builder description \(R = \{(x,y) : y = x^2,\, x \in \{1,2,3\}\}\) corresponds to which roster form?
questions.hint: Plug each allowed \(x\)-value into \(y=x^2\) one at a time.
distractor_logic: swaps the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) in each pair
uses \(y=2x\) instead of \(y=x^2\), a doubling rule rather than squaring
uses the identity relation \(y=x\) instead of the squaring rule actually given

questions.question: In an arrow diagram representing a relation \(R\) from \(A\) to \(B\), an arrow is drawn from \(a \in A\) to \(b \in B\) exactly when:
options: both \(a\) and \(b\) are the smallest elements of their sets
questions.explanation: An arrow from \(a\) to \(b\) means \(a\) is related to \(b\) under \(R\), i.e. the ordered pair \((a,b)\) belongs to \(R\).
questions.hint: The arrow's direction matches the order inside the ordered pair: from the first component to the second.
distractor_logic: reverses the direction of the pair, effectively drawing the arrow diagram for \(R^{-1}\) instead of \(R\)

questions.question: Given \(A = \{2,3,4\}\), \(B = \{3,4,5,6\}\), and the relation \(R = \{(x,y) : x \text{ divides } y\}\), the roster form of \(R\) is:
questions.hint: Go through each element of \(A\) in turn and check which elements of \(B\) it divides exactly.
distractor_logic: misses the valid pairs \((3,3)\) and \((4,4)\), perhaps by only checking \(2\) against \(B\)
lists all pairs starting with \(2\) regardless of whether divisibility holds, ignoring the actual condition
restricts to only equal-value pairs, missing that divisibility also includes pairs like \((2,4)\)

questions.question: A relation \(f\) from \(A\) to \(B\) is called a function if:
options: every element of \(A\) has at least one image in \(B\), possibly more than one
every element of \(A\) has exactly one image in \(B\)
every element of \(B\) has a pre-image in \(A\)
some elements of \(A\) may be left without an image
questions.explanation: A function requires that every element of the domain \(A\) maps to exactly one element of \(B\) — no element of \(A\) is left out, and none is mapped to more than one image.
questions.hint: Two conditions together: 'every element covered' AND 'exactly one image each'.
distractor_logic: describes the weaker requirement of a mere relation (some elements may have more than one image), not a function
describes surjectivity (onto), a separate property that isn't required just for \(f\) to be a function
directly contradicts the definition, which requires every element of \(A\) to have an image

questions.question: For a function \(f: A \to B\), the range of \(f\) is:
options: the set of elements in \(B\) that have no pre-image
the set of images \(\{f(a) : a \in A\}\), which is a subset of \(B\)
questions.explanation: The range is the collection of actual output values \(f(a)\) as \(a\) runs over \(A\) — it always satisfies \(\text{Range}(f) \subseteq B\), but need not equal all of \(B\).
questions.hint: Range = the set of values the function actually outputs, not the whole target set.
distractor_logic: describes the elements NOT in the range, essentially the opposite of what range means
wrongly assumes range always fills the entire co-domain, which fails whenever \(f\) is not onto
confuses range with the domain \(A\)

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes a function from a general relation?
options: Every function is a relation, but a relation is a function only if each element of the domain has a unique image
A function need not have a domain
A relation is always a function
A function is any subset of \(A \times B\)
questions.explanation: Every function is, by definition, a relation (a subset of \(A \times B\)). But a relation earns the stronger label 'function' only when every domain element maps to exactly one image, so functions form a special subclass of relations.
questions.hint: Ask: is 'function' a bigger or smaller category than 'relation'? Every function is a relation, but not conversely.
distractor_logic: contradicts the very definition of a function, which is built on having a well-defined domain
reverses the true containment — it is functions that are always relations, not the other way round
describes a general relation, not the stricter condition that makes something a function

questions.question: The 'vertical line test' applied to the graph of a relation is used to check whether the relation is:
questions.explanation: If every vertical line drawn through the graph meets it in at most one point, each \(x\)-value has at most one corresponding \(y\)-value — exactly the condition for the graph to represent a function.
questions.hint: A vertical line at a fixed \(x\) should cross the graph at most once for it to be a function.
distractor_logic: has no connection to the vertical line test
confuses the vertical line test (checks whether it's a function at all) with the horizontal line test, which instead checks one-one-ness

questions.question: If \(f: A \to B\) and an element \(a \in A\) is assigned two distinct images \(b_1, b_2 \in B\) with \(b_1 \neq b_2\), then:
options: \(f\) is a valid function as long as both \(b_1, b_2 \in B\)
\(f\) is not a function, since each domain element must have a unique image
\(f\) is a function only if \(A\) is finite
questions.explanation: A single element of the domain cannot map to two different images in a function — that violates the 'exactly one image' requirement, so \(f\) fails to be a function here (though it is still a valid relation).
questions.hint: This is precisely the situation the definition of a function rules out.
distractor_logic: wrongly treats having two distinct images as still acceptable for a function
introduces a finiteness condition that has nothing to do with whether images are unique
denies that this can happen, though it happens routinely for relations that are not functions

questions.topic: Real-Valued Functions — Identity, Constant & Polynomial Functions
questions.question: The identity function \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x) = x\) has domain and range:
options: domain and range both equal to \([0,\infty)\)
questions.explanation: Since \(f(x)=x\) maps every real number to itself, both the domain and the range of the identity function are all of \(\mathbb{R}\).
questions.hint: The output always equals the input, so the set of outputs is exactly the set of inputs.

questions.topic: Real-Valued Functions — Identity, Constant & Polynomial Functions
questions.question: A constant function \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) given by \(f(x) = c\) for a fixed real number \(c\) has range:
questions.explanation: No matter which \(x\) is chosen, \(f(x)\) always equals the same fixed value \(c\), so the range consists of that single value: \(\{c\}\).
questions.hint: Every input gives the exact same output for a constant function.
distractor_logic: confuses the range of a constant function with that of the identity function
